source.title: From Correlation to Cause: A Five-Stage Methodology for Feature Analysis in Transformer Language Models

page_placements.theme: Detection, decodability and recurrence do not establish selective control

record.tranche_reason: The study tests SAE feature extraction and causal effects in GPT-2, and finds that the interpreted feature subset accounts for only a minority of activation variance, that feature selection changes on held-out names, and that causal effects can degrade while firing remains stable.
record.gate_note: Rows cover SAE feature recovery, activation coverage, feature stability, and causal effects. Activation-patching circuit recovery concerns the IOI circuit rather than superposition geometry or feature units. Monitor ROC and cost results concern deployment performance, not the claim versions. Cited results from other work are not recorded as rows.
record.test_reason: The study trains an SAE on GPT-2 small IOI activations. It reports sparse, name-selective features (bears on V4) and tests their reconstruction coverage, causal force, redundancy and stability under distribution shift (bears on V5). It argues SAE features capture only one slice of a distributed code. It has no toy-model, neuron-polysemanticity or dimensionality analysis.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. Add that the authors place GPT-2 IOI in an 'intermediate causal regime', in which the SAE captures one slice of a distributed, redundant code. Add also that the patching-identified circuit, unlike the features' causal effects, transfers robustly across all three distribution shifts.
record.recipe_differences: The paper does not reproduce or apply the Toy Models of Superposition method; it uses SAE feature extraction and causal ablation on GPT-2 small.
record.method_sensitivity: Feature identities depend on the name distribution used for selection; causal effects vary across features and degrade under prompt-frame reformulation even when feature firing remains strong.

fits_no_version.finding: Selectivity ratio is anticorrelated with ablation effect across the ten name features (r = -0.56). The most selective features have the smallest causal effects.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The selectivity of an SAE feature does not predict its causal importance to model output.

fits_no_version.finding: The 15 interpreted name-selective features explain 30.7% of variance versus 99.7% for the full SAE.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Task-interpreted SAE features cover only a minority of the activation's content.

record.problems: The authors note that the model is small (GPT-2 small, 124 million parameters), the task is a single template-based IOI task, and the SAE is relatively small (1024 features and 3000 training steps). Reported findings are from one model and task; no uncertainty estimates are stated.
record.rows_left_out: Activation-patching circuit recovery and monitor calibration/composition/cost results are omitted because they do not measure the claim versions about superposition geometry or SAE representation units. The paper's cited results from other studies are also omitted.

untested.parts: No toy networks, sparsity sweep, phase transition or geometry.
No neuron-level polysemanticity or importance-based capacity allocation.
No alternative causes of polysemantic neurons.
No analysis of features spread across neurons. One small model, one layer and position, one template task.
No comparison across SAE seeds, sizes or architectures, so canonicality of the dictionary is untested. Completeness is tested only in-distribution on IOI.
No test of 1-D versus multi-dimensional features.

missing.what: Mean single-feature ablation drop of 0.67 logits on preferred-name prompts, essentially no effect on other prompts (a specificity control)
Monitor ROC-AUC of 1.00 for all ten features in-distribution and under OOD content and reformulation; SAE-monitor FPR rises from 1% to 3% to 4% (detection stability)
Per-name feature analysis inapplicable for multi-token names (Beatrice, Mortimer and similar)

record.verdict_notes: This is a methodology paper; superposition is not its framing. Its V5 bearing is indirect: it is about the causal and interpretive status of SAE features, not dictionary canonicality. The paper is internally inconsistent on in-distribution ablation drops: Table 1 gives Sid 0.34 and Adam 0.52, while Section 11.3 gives 0.85 and 0.78; the mean is 0.67 in Section 8.1 and 0.89 in Section 11. The SAE is small (1024 features). There is a single model and task, and no uncertainty estimates.

versions.untested_parts: No toy-network sweep of feature count versus dimension, sparsity-dependent geometric transition, or overlap geometry.
Does not test neuron polysemanticity or whether features compete for limited dimensions according to importance.
Does not test alternative causes of polysemantic neurons.
Tests SAE-recovered features in GPT-2 on IOI, not feature spreading across neurons or generalization to other models and tasks.

Tests the interpreted SAE subset, selected feature identities, and some robustness properties in one model and task; does not establish completeness or canonicality across models, tasks, or training settings.
Does not compare one-dimensional feature directions with multidimensional features.

rows.subject: GPT-2 small
rows.operation_detail: Measured which SAE features dominated for names excluded from the 16-name SAE training pool.

conditions.value: Anna, Mark, Lucy, Peter, Emma, Tim, Kate, Paul

rows.measure: Dominant SAE feature identity
rows.value: Feature 103 dominated for Anna, Mark, Tim, Kate; feature 179 for Lucy, Emma; feature 181 for Peter, Paul. None of the top-10 in-distribution selective features was dominant for any held-out name.
rows.note: The paper says the SAE learned other features that surfaced for held-out names, so the training-distribution feature selection did not identify the only comparable features.
rows.check: Shows that selection on training names misses the generic name features (103, 179, 181) present in the same SAE. This bears on which features are canonical for a role, not on SAE instability across training runs.

source_check.correct: Features 103, 179 and 181 dominate for the listed held-out names; all belong to the same trained SAE. V5 state: cannot_determine. This establishes distribution-dependent feature selection, without testing dictionary canonicality or instability.
source_check.problem: Different inputs activating different existing features does not establish a failure of complete, stable, canonical units.

relation.reason: Its own experiments measure sparse recoverable features, reconstruction coverage and feature-firing stability, directly bearing on V4 and tested aspects of V5.

tranche.reason: The paper explicitly argues that the SAE basis only approximates the distributed code and that interpreted features provide incomplete explanations. This supports an argument-based T5 classification, although several listed causal results do not directly test V5's stated properties.

source_check.notes: The text contains unreconciled ablation differences across Table 1 and Section 11, including Sid, Adam, Mary and mean effects. Section 7.1 also calls 1,024 features a 4× expansion over 768 dimensions; retain the stated dimensions, not that expansion claim.

statements.correction: GPT-2 small; fifteen selected name features ablated; mean logit difference +3.71 to +3.33; accuracy 100.0% to 98.4%; selected subset not necessary; full-dictionary completeness and canonicality not determined by this intervention.
statements.problem: The GPT-2 ablation result and selected-subset interpretation are correct, but the challenges label overstates what this study establishes about V5. Selected-feature necessity is distinct from full-dictionary completeness, stability and canonicality.
